title: Greatest Tail of a String
statement:
You get a lowercase string s. Among all of its non-empty substrings, return the one that comes last in dictionary order.

Dictionary order compares character by character; if one string is a prefix of the other, the shorter one comes first.

examples.why: The answer starts with the biggest letter, c. Extending it never hurts, so it runs to the end of the string.
Both c's are candidates. After the first c comes a, after the second comes b, so the second start wins.
"z" is a prefix of "zaz", so the longer one is greater.

constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
hints: The answer is always a suffix: if a substring is the greatest, extending it to the end only makes it greater. So which suffix is largest?
Comparing every suffix with the best one costs O(n²) on inputs like "aaaa…ab". Can a failed comparison rule out more than one start at once?
Keep two candidate starts i < j and compare s[i + k] with s[j + k]. If they differ after k equal characters, every start in the losing range i..i + k (or j..j + k) also loses. Jump past it.

explain.intuition:
Any substring is a prefix of the suffix that starts at the same position, and a prefix is never greater than the whole string. So the answer is the largest suffix. Comparing suffixes naively is O(n) per comparison, and O(n²) in total for strings like "aaaa…ab".

The trick is to make each mismatch eliminate a whole range. Keep a best start i and a challenger j, and let k be how many characters already matched. If s[i + k] < s[j + k], then not only i loses but every start i + t for t ≤ k: it would face j + t, which matches it up to the same failing character. So i jumps past i + k. The mirror case moves j past j + k. Each jump discards at least k + 1 starts, which keeps the total work linear.
steps: While j + k < n: if s[i + k] = s[j + k], increase k.
If s[i + k] < s[j + k]: set i = max(i + k + 1, j), j = i + 1, k = 0.
If s[i + k] > s[j + k]: set j = j + k + 1, k = 0.
pitfalls: Returning the longest run of the largest letter, or the first occurrence of it. In "cacb" the second c wins.
Moving i only one step after a loss. That is correct but drops back to O(n²) on long repeated patterns.
Setting i = i + k + 1 without taking the max with j. The new i can then land before j, on starts that already lost to i, and the loop redoes work it could skip.

solutions.title: Compare every suffix
solutions.idea: The answer is the largest suffix. Compare each suffix with the best so far.

solutions.title: Two candidate starts with skipping
solutions.idea: Compare the suffixes at i and j character by character. When they differ after k matches, the loser and the k starts after it are all out, so skip them.

followups: Return the smallest suffix instead. Can you reuse the same loop?
How does this relate to finding the lexicographically smallest rotation of a string?
